He said the violence "is one part of a series of a crusade war against Islam and these air strikes are a gift from Obama before he takes office, and (Egyptian President) Hosni Mubarak, that traitor, is the main partner in your siege and killing." The message, posted Tuesday on various Islamist Web sites with a picture of al-Zawahiri next to an image of a wounded child, urges militants to rally against Israel. "My Muslim brothers and mujahedeens in Gaza and all over Palestine, with the help of God we are with you in the battle, we will direct our strikes against the crusader Jewish coalition wherever we can." It was Obama's first public reaction to the ongoing fighting between Israel and Hamas militants in Gaza, which began with Israeli air strikes 11 days ago. He reiterated that only one president can speak for the United States at a time. "Starting at the beginning of our administration, we are going to engage effectively and consistently to try to resolve the conflicts that exist in the Middle East," Obama said. CNN Senior International Correspondent Nic Robertson said the al Qaeda message speaks to al-Zawahiri's cause in two ways: It bashes the new U.S. president before he takes office and it criticizes Mubarak, who has drawn al-Zawahiri's ire for not allowing goods and aid through Egypt's border with Gaza. Robertson, who is reporting from the Israeli-Gaza border, noted on CNN's "Situation Room" that al-Zawahiri got the message out quickly -- "within 12 days, that's very fast." # Al Qaeda's Zawahiri Criticizes Obama, Israeli Assault on Gaza

Al Qaeda's second-in-command, Ayman al-Zawahiri, released an audio message condemning Israel's military operation in Gaza while launching pointed criticism at U.S. President-elect Barack Obama, according to a recording that appeared on Islamist websites.

In the message, al-Zawahiri characterized the Israeli offensive as part of what he described as a broader campaign against Muslims, and he sought to link the incoming American administration to Israeli policy. The al Qaeda deputy leader referred to Obama in derogatory terms and argued that the change in U.S. leadership would not alter what he portrayed as American hostility toward the Muslim world.

## Attempt to Exploit Gaza Conflict

Terrorism analysts said the message represented an effort by al Qaeda to capitalize on anger in the Muslim world over the mounting Palestinian casualties in Gaza. The Israeli operation, launched in response to rocket fire from the territory, has drawn widespread condemnation across the region.

By inserting itself into the Gaza conflict rhetorically, al Qaeda appeared to be attempting to position itself as a defender of Palestinians, despite the group having little operational presence in the territory, which is controlled by Hamas.

## Targeting the Incoming President

The decision to single out Obama, who had not yet taken office, suggested al Qaeda was moving quickly to define the new president in the eyes of potential recruits and sympathizers. Al-Zawahiri's remarks appeared designed to preempt any goodwill the historic election might generate in Muslim-majority countries.

The authenticity of the recording could not be independently verified, though the message was distributed through channels typically used by al Qaeda for official communications, and the voice resembled that of previous al-Zawahiri messages.

## Background

Al-Zawahiri, an Egyptian physician who became one of Osama bin Laden's closest associates, has served as the primary public voice of al Qaeda, frequently releasing audio and video statements addressing current events. His messages have often sought to connect regional conflicts to the group's global agenda.

U.S. officials have historically downplayed such recordings while continuing to monitor them for intelligence value and any indication of operational planning.

---

# Al-Zawahiri Audio Message Addresses Gaza Conflict, Denounces Mubarak

*A journalistic account of an audio recording attributed to the al-Qaeda leader*

## Overview

An audio message approximately 10 minutes in length, attributed to al-Qaeda's then-second-in-command Ayman al-Zawahiri, surfaced during a period of intense fighting between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip. The recording followed a pattern typical of al-Qaeda's media output during that era, in which the group's leadership sought to insert itself rhetorically into ongoing regional conflicts to claim relevance and rally support.

## Context of the Recording

Messages of this type were commonly released through al-Qaeda's media arm, As-Sahab, and distributed via jihadist web forums before being picked up by international news organizations. Intelligence analysts and media outlets would typically work to authenticate such recordings by comparing voice patterns to previous confirmed messages, though independent verification often remained difficult.

The timing of such messages—released during active hostilities in Gaza—was widely interpreted by observers as an effort by al-Qaeda to capitalize on Muslim anger over civilian casualties and to position the organization as a defender of the Palestinian cause, despite Hamas maintaining organizational and ideological independence from al-Qaeda.

## Key Themes Attributed to the Message

**Address to Gazans:** The recording reportedly directed its message to Muslims in Gaza, expressing solidarity with Palestinians enduring the Israeli military operation. Messages of this nature typically framed the suffering in Gaza as part of a broader narrative of a war against Islam.

**Condemnation of Hosni Mubarak:** A significant portion of the message reportedly targeted Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak. Al-Zawahiri, himself Egyptian and a longtime opponent of the Egyptian government, frequently denounced Mubarak as a collaborator with Israel and Western powers. Criticism often centered on Egypt's handling of the Rafah border crossing, accusing the Mubarak government of complicity in the blockade of Gaza by keeping the crossing closed to Palestinians seeking to flee or receive aid.

**Reaction to Israeli Operations:** The message reacted to the Israeli military campaign against Hamas, condemning the airstrikes and ground operations while calling on Muslims worldwide to support the Palestinians through action rather than words.

## Analytical Perspective

Observers and counterterrorism analysts frequently noted the underlying tension in such appeals. While al-Zawahiri sought to champion the Palestinian cause, al-Qaeda and Hamas differed significantly in ideology, strategy, and organizational structure. Hamas operated as a Palestinian nationalist-Islamist movement with governance responsibilities, while al-Qaeda pursued a transnational jihadist agenda. Some analysts interpreted al-Zawahiri's messaging as an implicit criticism of Hamas for participating in elections and pursuing political legitimacy—approaches al-Qaeda rejected.

## Media and Governmental Response

Recordings attributed to al-Zawahiri generally received substantial coverage from international news agencies, which reported on their content while noting the challenges of verification. Government officials often downplayed such messages as propaganda attempts to remain relevant, particularly as al-Qaeda's core leadership faced increasing pressure.

---

*Note: This article describes the general characteristics, context, and reported content of such audio messages based on established patterns of al-Qaeda communications during this period. Specific claims about any individual recording should be verified against primary reporting from the relevant date, as details regarding exact wording, release channels, and authentication varied by incident.*

# Al Qaeda Deputy Releases Audio Message on Gaza; Obama Breaks Silence on Conflict

**By Staff Writer**

Al Qaeda's second-in-command, Ayman al-Zawahiri, released a new audio recording addressing the ongoing conflict in Gaza, according to an online message posted on Islamist websites frequently used to distribute al Qaeda propaganda. The recording emerged as the death toll from Israeli military operations in the Gaza Strip continued to climb.

## The Audio Message

In the recording, which was accompanied by a still image of Zawahiri, the Egyptian-born deputy to Osama bin Laden sought to capitalize on regional anger over the Gaza offensive. Zawahiri characterized the Israeli operation as part of a broader campaign against Muslims and called on followers to respond with attacks.

Zawahiri directed harsh criticism at Arab governments, particularly Egypt, accusing regional leaders of complicity with Israel and the West. He specifically denounced Egyptian authorities for their handling of the border crossing with Gaza, framing established governments as having betrayed the Palestinian cause.

The al Qaeda figure urged Muslims worldwide to strike targets associated with what he described as a coalition of enemies, seeking to portray the terror network as a defender of Palestinians—a population with which al Qaeda has historically had limited operational connection.

Analysts have long noted that al Qaeda attempts to exploit high-profile conflicts involving Muslim populations for recruitment and propaganda purposes, even in theaters where the group maintains no meaningful presence. The Palestinian territories have historically been dominated by other militant factions, including Hamas, which al Qaeda-affiliated ideologues have at times criticized.

The authenticity of the recording could not be independently verified, though it appeared on websites typically used for such releases and bore the production hallmarks of al Qaeda's media arm.

## Obama Comments on the Conflict

Separately, President-elect Barack Obama offered his first substantive public remarks on the Gaza situation, breaking a relative silence he had maintained by repeatedly invoking the principle that the United States has "only one president at a time."

Facing mounting questions about his views on the escalating violence, Obama expressed concern over the mounting civilian casualties on both sides of the conflict. He emphasized that the loss of civilian life, whether Palestinian or Israeli, was a source of deep concern.

Obama reiterated his commitment to engaging on Middle East policy immediately upon taking office, signaling that resolving the broader Israeli-Palestinian conflict would be a priority for his incoming administration. He stopped short of criticizing the outgoing administration's approach or laying out specific policy prescriptions, maintaining his stated position of deferring to the sitting president on active foreign policy matters until his inauguration.

The president-elect's careful comments reflected the delicate diplomatic position he occupied during the transition period, as he sought to avoid undermining current U.S. policy while acknowledging the gravity of the deteriorating situation.

## Background

The conflict began after Israel launched military operations aimed at halting rocket fire from Gaza into southern Israel. The offensive drew international attention and prompted diplomatic efforts to broker a ceasefire, even as the humanitarian situation in the densely populated territory deteriorated.

The dual developments—a propaganda push from al Qaeda's leadership and the first remarks from the incoming American president—underscored the international dimensions of a conflict being closely watched across the Middle East and around the world.

---

*Note: This article is written in a general news style. For a publication-ready piece, specific dates, casualty figures, direct quotations, and additional sourcing would be verified and incorporated.*
